A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ERA study, retaining its objective, theoretical foundations and original molecular experiments. The complete main texts, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison despite the changed title and experimental scope.

before.justification: V1 reports original molecular-generation experiments, GPT-2 sentiment alignment and LLaMA2 weak-to-strong alignment, with results and examples in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains original molecular results and adds ERA experiments on kinase-targeted generation, molecular DPO comparison and TrpB protein-sequence optimization. Its ERA results are original even where comparator scores are reproduced from cited work.

M1.justification: The ERA objective, beta/gamma controls and supplied loss implementation remain unchanged. V2 adds a limited adaptation to bidirectional ESM3: four protein mutation sites are unmasked simultaneously, and alignment pairs come from randomly generated mutants (Appendix F). V1 demonstrates autoregressive molecular and text generation.

E1.justification: V2 retains the ChEMBL/RDKit molecular-property tasks, adds GSK3β and JNK3 optimization and four-site TrpB protein-sequence optimization, and removes the IMDb sentiment and Anthropic Helpful and Harmless language-alignment experiments. These substantially change the evaluated tasks and domains.

E2.justification: V2 adds kinase comparisons with MolRL-MGPT, GFlowNet, GraphGA, JT-VAE and REINVENT in Table 1, using reproduced baseline scores; Table S7 compares sample efficiency with REINVENT and GraphGA. The LLaMA2 DPO comparison disappears, while DPO is newly evaluated against ERA on molecular QED optimization in Figure S6.

E3.justification: New kinase protocols evaluate the top 100 valid, novel and unique molecules from 20,000 samples and introduce IntDiv and top-10 AUC with explicit oracle-call filtering. The protein experiment uses 512 random mutants, four specified mutation sites and EVmutation evaluation. Figure S6 adds checkpoint evaluation with 20,000 samples per checkpoint. Existing RDKit settings are retained; the language-evaluation protocols are removed.

E4.justification: V2 adds a DPO-versus-ERA analysis of chemical validity and QED across training checkpoints, protein beta sensitivity, sampling-efficiency curves and Glide docking case studies. It removes the language-specific beta/gamma analyses and generated-response examples. The original molecular diversity, validity and multi-property analyses remain.

E5.justification: V1 Figure 5 briefly notes error bars too small to display without specifying seed counts. V2 Tables 1 and S7 report averages across five random seeds with ± values, and Figure S13 displays five seed-specific curves. Figure S6 additionally reports one-standard-deviation bands across sampled QED scores. This substantially expands statistical reporting; it does not establish additional runs for retained experiments.

E6.justification: The retained molecular plots and validity values are unchanged, but language results, including the reported greater-than-90% unsafe-content reduction, disappear. New Table 1 reports ERA scores of 0.996 for GSK3β and 0.987 for JNK3, versus MolRL-MGPT's 1.000 and 0.961, with lower IntDiv for ERA on both. Table S7 adds ERA AUC scores of 0.985 and 0.989. New findings also cover DPO validity collapse and high-EVmutation protein generation.

T1.justification: The conditional-equivalence definitions, Gibbs–Boltzmann minimizer proof, gradient expressions and PPO/DPO derivations are retained through relocation from v1 Section 3 and Appendix B to v2 Appendices B–C. Duplicated loss exposition adds no new argument. The added IntDiv formula documents an empirical metric without changing the theoretical results.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution paragraph and conclusion replace claims of successful general-language and weak-to-strong alignment with claims about generating desirable protein mutants. V1's highlighted unsafe-content reduction is removed. The central claims about explicit rewards, the Gibbs–Boltzmann target and separately controlled entropy and regularization remain.

C2.justification: V2 removes interpretations concerning text coherence and weak-to-strong supervision, and adds discussion of sampling efficiency, docking-pose plausibility and directed-evolution applicability. It explicitly qualifies protein fitness as computationally assessed without experimental validation. Reward-model and synthesizability limitations remain, as does a limited-DPO-tuning caveat accompanying the new molecular comparison.

D1.justification: Appendices E.4 and F add TDC oracle details, kinase fine-tuning selection and dataset sizes, 40,000-molecule alignment datasets, optimizer settings, ESM3 masking procedures, mutation positions and protein sampling details. The detailed GPT-2/LLaMA procedures are removed. The supplied ERA loss code, repository-access statements and hardware disclosure remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands its positioning in molecular benchmarking and protein engineering through sources on docking, sample efficiency, ESM3, EVmutation, directed evolution and protein DPO. It removes references specific to GPT-2, LLaMA2, sentiment analysis and weak-to-strong generalization. Section 1.1's basic positioning against PPO and DPO is largely retained.

P1.justification: The title and empirical narrative are refocused, the main theoretical-analysis section moves into Appendices B–C, and the experimental and concluding sections are reorganized around kinase and protein applications. Appendix C also repeats existing loss-function exposition. This is substantial structural revision despite extensive retained wording.

P2.justification: V2 adds kinase result tables, docking images, protein distributions, checkpoint plots and sampling-efficiency curves, while removing language-result figures and response tables. V1 Figure 4 moves to Figure S10. Retained chemical graphics are enlarged or relocated, and validity tables are widened and consolidated without changing their values.

improvement.justification: V2 better supports the central chemical-design contribution through kinase comparisons, novelty/diversity evaluation, five-seed reporting and Glide checks, while preserving the theory and original molecular evidence. The gain is limited by unresolved comparison issues: sample-efficiency reporting counts post-alignment oracle calls without establishing comparable total costs including the 40,000-molecule alignment-data stage, and DPO tuning remains limited. Protein results provide useful additional scope but remain computational proxies, while the earlier language validation is removed.
